name: Using very few words
distractors: Taking a long time to answer
example: His laconic reply was “No.”

name: Frank and honest
example: She was candid about why the plan had failed.

name: Very attentive to detail
example: His meticulous notes included the time and place of every interview.

name: Having mixed feelings
example: Lena felt ambivalent about moving closer to work and farther from her friends.

name: Seeming believable
example: His explanation sounded plausible until I checked the dates.

name: Difficult to find, catch, or understand
distractors: Easy to overlook because it is ordinary
example: A permanent solution remained elusive despite months of testing.

name: Focused on what works in practice
distractors: Driven by a desire to innovate
example: She took a pragmatic approach and fixed the leaky window before replacing the trim.

name: Quick and lacking thoroughness
example: A cursory glance at the menu missed the specials printed on the back.

name: Occurring at irregular intervals
example: Sporadic showers sent us indoors twice that afternoon.

name: Careful about spending or using resources
distractors: Willing to pay more for quality
example: A frugal cook, he made stock from vegetable scraps.

name: Using more words than necessary
example: The verbose instructions took three paragraphs to explain how to plug it in.

name: Cautious about possible danger or trouble
distractors: Eager to take a calculated risk
example: I was wary of opening an attachment from an unknown sender.

name: Persistent and unwilling to give up
distractors: Quick to recover after a setback
example: The tenacious reporter kept requesting the records for months.

name: Clear and leaving no room for doubt
example: The inspector gave an unequivocal answer: the bridge had to close.

name: Ordinary and unremarkable
example: They chatted about mundane things like groceries and laundry.

name: Unnecessary because it duplicates something
example: The second reminder was redundant because everyone had already received the first.

name: Fair and without favoritism
distractors: Willing to compromise on every point
example: They asked an impartial referee to settle the dispute.

name: Understood without being directly expressed
example: They had a tacit agreement to leave the office door open.

name: Little known or hard to understand
distractors: Easy to explain in simple terms
example: The archive held an obscure pamphlet about a forgotten local election.

name: Able to recover after difficulty
distractors: Unwilling to adjust to changing conditions
example: The resilient plants put out new leaves after the frost.

name: Lasting only a short time
distractors: Continuing as long as conditions stay stable
example: The headache was transient and faded before lunch.

name: Producing a large amount of work or output
distractors: Starting many projects and finishing few
Working steadily on a single project
example: The prolific author published six novels in four years.

name: Examine closely and carefully
example: Please scrutinize the bill before we pay it.

name: Based on personal accounts or isolated examples
distractors: Based on an established mathematical proof
example: The evidence was anecdotal: three customers said their packages arrived early.

name: Detect or recognize something that is hard to notice
distractors: Conceal something that others might notice
Predict something from a familiar pattern
example: In the fog I could barely discern the outline of the pier.

name: Make suffering or a problem less severe
distractors: Find the underlying cause of a problem
example: A cold compress helped alleviate the swelling.

name: Support a claim with additional evidence
distractors: Repeat a claim without checking it
Withdraw a claim after an objection
example: Two independent witnesses could corroborate her account.

name: Make an existing problem worse
distractors: Bring a hidden problem to light
Make a problem easier to tolerate
Replace one problem with an unrelated one
example: The detour threatened to exacerbate congestion downtown.

name: Show that someone was right or free from blame
distractors: Forgive someone without deciding who was right
Punish someone for breaking a rule
Explain someone's motives without defending them
example: The newly recovered logs helped vindicate the engineer.

name: Bring opposing accounts or views into agreement
distractors: Choose one account without considering the other
Collect every account in one place
Keep two accounts from being compared
example: The clerk managed to reconcile the receipts with the cash in the drawer.
